silo_relevance: This paper matters for simulation_monte_carlo because it gives a noise-aware sampling framework with explicit overhead and variance bounds for extracting reliable estimates from noisy quantum devices. Its CVaR-based bounds and sampling-cost analysis are directly relevant to Monte Carlo-style estimation workflows, especially when the quantum routine is used to approximate expectation values or sample good outcomes under hardware noise.

key_points.point: Noise-aware sampling overhead is quantified as a square-root scaling in the aggregate noise parameter.
key_points.silo_note: Monte Carlo methods depend on repeated sampling; this result tells you how much extra sampling is needed to preserve useful output statistics when the quantum sampler is noisy.

key_points.point: CVaR of noisy samples provides provable bounds on noise-free expectation values.
key_points.silo_note: For simulation tasks that estimate expectations, this is the most directly relevant result: it turns noisy sample averages into bounded estimators rather than requiring exact unbiased recovery.

key_points.point: Estimator variance is explicitly bounded, with improved scaling in Bernoulli/normal-like cases.
key_points.silo_note: Monte Carlo simulation is only useful if estimator variance is controlled; these bounds indicate how the uncertainty of the quantum postprocessing behaves as sampling becomes more aggressive.

key_points.point: Problem structure can tighten bounds through filtering and post-selection.
key_points.silo_note: In simulation settings where valid outcomes satisfy known constraints, filtering can reduce wasted samples and sharpen the interval in which the estimated quantity must lie.

key_points.point: The approach is experimentally validated but can be shot-expensive at larger scale.
key_points.silo_note: For Monte Carlo-style financial simulation, practical usefulness depends on sample cost; the paper shows the method works on hardware but also flags that required shots may be impractical for larger instances.
